turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mrs Adeyemi, have a seat. How have you been getting on at home?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm perfectly alright. I don't know why she's hauled me down here, if I'm honest.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's not alright. Her ankles have been up like puddings, and she has to stop halfway up the stairs.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Puddings. They're a bit puffy by the evening, that's all. Hardly a crisis.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): A bit puffy by evening, noted. When she says you stop on the stairs, do you get short of breath at all?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I just take my time. I'm not breathless.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is, though. She sits on the stair with her hand on her chest. Most days, going up.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I sit because my knees are old, not because I can't get air. You're making a meal of it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. In your own time, when did the puffiness actually start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you. Last winter, or the one before. It comes and goes. Not worth pinning down.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's been worse these past three weeks, evenings especially. Her shoes won't go on.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are you sleeping? Any waking up gasping, or needing more pillows?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep like a log. One pillow, same as ever. She's the one fussing at night.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does cough a bit once she lies down. Dry, not a chesty one.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Everyone coughs. It's the heating. It's nothing.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest with all this?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. I keep saying I'm fine.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's untangle the tablets, then. The box looks as if it's got away from you. Who fills it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do. I live in. Every Sunday I do the dosette. Morning she's got the water tablet and the heart one, and there's a little white one at night that isn't labelled.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The water one makes me traipse to the loo, so sometimes I don't bother. And that little white one, I couldn't tell you. Might be a vitamin for all I know.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The water tablet — do you know its real name and the strength?

[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Furosemide, forty milligrams, one in the morning. That's what the chemist box says. There's another blister that looks the same, and I think I've been dropping two in some mornings without meaning to.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't take two. I take one, if I take it. She's counting the same tablet twice, that's the muddle.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So it's one furosemide, forty milligrams, not two different water tablets. And the heart one?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Bisoprolol. The packet in the cupboard says two point five milligrams.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, mine's the half. One point two five. The hospital doctor halved it. She's still on the old dose, if you ask me.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't guess the bisoprolol today. I'll want that hospital letter before anyone changes it. Has anything been stopped?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The other doctor stopped the ramipril. Said it was knocking my kidneys about. I don't take it.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril five milligrams. It came out of the box ages ago.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when was that, roughly?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before. I haven't a clue, really. Whenever that appointment was.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): They did print a simvastatin script once as well, but she never swallowed a single one. I didn't even pick up the repeat.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Cholesterol rubbish. My sister's the one on metformin, for her sugar. She's forever pushing her biotin on me for my hair. I haven't touched it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your sister's metformin and her biotin stay hers. We won't put either on your list. Anything else — inhalers, shop-bought bits?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't go in for all that. Paracetamol now and then, if my head's a bit off. That's the lot.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does have the paracetamol, maybe twice a week. Five hundred milligrams, two tablets. I buy them.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I look at your ankles and have a listen to your chest?

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's pitting swelling on both sides, up to the mid-shin. Chest is clear, no crackles. Pulse is seventy-six, blood pressure one hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-four.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Clear chest. There you are. I told you I was fine.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): A clear chest is reassuring, but that swelling is proper fluid. I think this is most likely your body holding on to fluid, possibly the heart not quite keeping up. I can't be certain until we do a few tests.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to change the water tablet. Furosemide forty milligrams in the morning and again at lunchtime, instead of the single dose. Leave the bisoprolol exactly as it is until I see the letter.
[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Morning and lunch, forty each. I'll redo the dosette tonight, and I won't double it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): More time in the loo. Wonderful. If I feel like skipping it, I still might.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd really like you to take both doses while we sort this out. I'll send you for bloods, kidney function and a BNP, and an ECG today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods. I had bloods last winter or whenever. Waste of time.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a waste. It tells me the higher dose is safe for your kidneys. If the swelling hasn't eased in two weeks, we might arrange a heart scan.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her there. Do you want her weighed at home?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes please, each morning after the loo, and jot the number down. Ease off the very salty food if you can. Come back and see me in a fortnight with the weights and the results. If she's suddenly much more breathless, or the swelling shoots up before then, don't wait, ring the surgery or 999 if she can't speak in sentences.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, if I must. I'm still not ill.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Tablet name is unclear, but caregiver says night-time frequency; she can still identify it as a little white one.
bad.text: Neither the patient nor the carer can name the little white night-time tablet. (type=incomplete_medication_name, related_entities=medications[3], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Patient denied shortness of breath: 'I'm not breathless'; she said she stops/sits on the stairs because her knees are old, not because she cannot get air.
Ankle swelling has worsened over the past three weeks and is worse in the evenings, with shoes not fitting on because of the swelling (reported by caregiver).
Patient denied orthopnoea more fully by saying she sleeps like a log and uses one pillow, same as ever.
Current furosemide adherence issue: patient sometimes does not take the morning furosemide because it makes her urinate frequently ('traipse to the loo').

Possible medication administration error detail: caregiver thinks she may have been putting two furosemide tablets into some mornings by mistake because there was another similar blister pack; patient disputes this and says she takes one if she takes it.
Bisoprolol dose is recorded incompletely/wrongly: caregiver said packet says 2.5 mg, but patient said her actual dose is half that, 1.25 mg, after the hospital doctor halved it.
Doctor explicitly said not to guess or change the bisoprolol dose today and wanted the hospital letter before any change.
Ramipril was stopped because it was affecting her kidneys ('knocking my kidneys about').
Simvastatin was printed once but the patient never took any and the repeat was not collected.
Patient specifically said she has not taken metformin or biotin; these belong to her sister and should not be on her medication list.
Patient denied using inhalers or other over-the-counter/shop-bought medicines apart from occasional paracetamol.
Chest examination included that the chest was clear, not just 'no crackles'.
Heart scan was described as being considered if the swelling has not eased in two weeks.
Follow-up was to return in a fortnight with the home weight record and the test results.
Safety-netting was more specific: call 999 if she is so breathless that she cannot speak in sentences.
